title: Not All RFCs are Standards
summary: Explains that publication as an RFC does not make a document an Internet Standard. Many RFCs are informational, experimental, or historic, and only those that go through the standards process carry that status.

plainLanguage.summary: An RFC is a document in the RFC publication series, but it is not automatically an Internet Standard. RFC 1796 explains the status labels and separate STD numbers that identify standards.

questions: what is the difference between an rfc and a standard
subtitle: An explanation of why publication in the RFC series does not make a document a standard.

tldr.problem: Readers may mistake any RFC for an Internet Standard, even though the RFC series also publishes informational, experimental, and historic documents.
tldr.mechanism: The memo explains the status labels used for RFCs and the separate STD numbers assigned to Internet Standards. It argues for clearer status information while keeping one archive.
tldr.outcome: RFC 1796 is an Informational memo explaining the IAB's 1995 position: publication is not standardization, and status should be made clear.

facts.label: Standards Track levels
facts.value: Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, Internet Standard

today: RFC 1796 is an Informational memo, and the unit metadata lists no RFC as obsoleting or updating it. Its description of RFC statuses and STD numbers states the IAB's position in April 1995.

sections.title: Publication Does Not Mean Standardization
sections.content:
The RFC series is the publication channel for Internet standards documents and other publications from the IESG, IAB, and Internet community. RFC 1796 addresses the misconception that publication as an RFC itself gives a document status as an Internet Standard. The memo says it does not.

Each RFC has a status in relation to the standardization process. The statuses named in this memo are Informational, Experimental, Standards Track, or Historic. Standards Track includes Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, and Internet Standard.
sections.plainLanguage: An RFC number tells you which document you are reading, not whether it is a standard. Check the RFC's status to see how it relates to the standards process.

sections.title: How RFC and STD Numbers Differ
sections.content:
The memo says an RFC's status appears on its first page and in the periodic Internet Official Protocol Standards document, called STD 1. When a specification becomes an Internet Standard, it receives an additional STD number but keeps its RFC number and place in the RFC series.

RFC numbers identify documents; STD numbers identify protocols. The relationship is not one-to-one because a standard protocol may be specified by more than one document. To make status easier to see, the IAB proposed using STD numbers in cross-references between standards-track documents and adding an HTML version of STD 1.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC numbers identify documents, while STD numbers identify standard protocols. One standard may be described by multiple RFCs, so the numbers do not match one for one.

sections.title: Why the RFC Series Keeps One Archive
sections.content:
The IAB favored a single archival series because documents are easier to find and retrieve when they share one publication system. The memo says smaller subseries can disappear from the network and that there was no evidence that a different publication scheme would reduce confusion. Its proposed response was to publicize the status of standards more clearly.

The RFC series also includes specifications developed outside the IETF standards process, including experimental work, privately developed protocols, and proposals that did not reach the needed consensus. The IAB's position was that making such documents available was better than leaving them inaccessible in private repositories. The security section says security issues are not discussed.
sections.plainLanguage: The IAB supported keeping standards and other technical documents in one archive, with clear status labels. Publishing a document makes it easier to find; it does not make the document a standard.
